prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "SOUTHERN CO" (ticker SO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Southern Company
result.industry: Regulated electric and natural gas utility
markets: Regulated retail electricity in Georgia, Alabama and southeastern Mississippi
Regulated natural gas distribution in four states (Illinois, Georgia, Virginia, Tennessee)
Power supply for data centers and other large loads in the Southeast

mission.statement: Providing clean, safe, reliable and affordable energy with excellent service is our mission.
mission.source: Southern Company corporate profile / press-release boilerplate (3BL Media company profile)
mission.plain: Give people power that is clean, safe, dependable and not too expensive, and treat them well.

about.plain: Southern Company makes electricity and delivers it to homes and businesses in Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi. It also pipes natural gas to homes in four states. It owns big power plants, including the newest nuclear reactors built in the US, plus gas, solar and water-powered plants. Because it is the only power company allowed in most of its areas, the state decides how much it can charge.
about.customers: About 9 million homes, businesses, factories and, more and more, giant data centers in the Southeast and beyond.
about.everyday: When someone in Atlanta or Birmingham flips on a light, charges a phone or turns on a gas stove, the energy very likely comes from a Southern Company utility.

money.plain: electricity for Alabama homes and businesses
natural gas delivered to about 4.4 million customers
power sold wholesale to other utilities under long contracts

money.part: Power for data centers and other large loads
money.plain: long-term contracts to power huge computing centers

result.summary: Southern has a durable, government-granted advantage: it is the exclusive electric utility across most of Georgia, Alabama and southeastern Mississippi, so rivals cannot build competing grids there. The flip side is that regulators set its prices and returns, so the moat protects steady earnings rather than allowing outsized profits; the data-center boom (10 GW contracted, a 75 GW pipeline) gives it unusual growth for a utility.

pricingPower.evidence: Prices are set by state commissions, not the market: the Georgia PSC approved freezing Georgia Power base rates through at least 2028 (July 2025), yet Southern still grew revenue 10.6% to $29.6B in 2025 and retail kWh sales 1.6%, because customers have no alternative supplier; it can recover prudent costs (e.g. Vogtle, storm costs) but cannot raise prices at will.

moats.evidence: Its real intangible asset is its exclusive state franchises and regulatory relationships rather than a consumer brand; it was ranked No. 1 among electric and gas utilities in FORTUNE's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies.
Residential and most business customers in its electric territories legally cannot switch electricity supplier, and data centers sign minimum 15-year contracts.
A customer gains nothing from more customers joining the grid; there is no network effect in the economic sense.

With about 9 million customers, 103 power plants and an $81B five-year capital plan, it can finance and build large generation (including the only new US nuclear units, Vogtle 3 and 4) more cheaply than smaller utilities.
Its service territories support only one grid; duplicating transmission and distribution would be uneconomic, which is why states grant it a regulated monopoly.
It is an incumbent regulated utility, not a new business model that incumbents cannot copy.

Completing Vogtle Units 3 and 4 (Unit 4 entered commercial operation on April 29, 2024) gave it rare US experience building and running new nuclear reactors, though the project was years late and over budget.
Exclusive franchise territories in fast-growing Southeast states plus existing nuclear, hydro and transmission assets and sites that a new entrant could not replicate.

customers.evidence: Customers stay because they must (regulated customer count rose 0.8% to 9,005K in 2025), while satisfaction is mixed: Southern was named the top US energy company in Newsweek's 2025 Most Trustworthy Companies list, but bill increases tied to Vogtle and data-center build-out draw political criticism in Georgia.

talent.evidence: About 30,000 employees; Southern ranked No. 1 among electric and gas utilities in FORTUNE's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies and is a steady, well-paid employer, but it is not on top-tier 'best places to work' lists that tech firms dominate.

product.evidence: Electricity is a commodity; Southern's distinction is reliability and a diverse fleet (nuclear, gas, hydro, solar) including the first new US nuclear units in decades (Vogtle 3 in 2023, Vogtle 4 in 2024), but customers judge mainly on price and reliability.

competitors.name: Duke Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Neighboring Southeast regulated utility (Carolinas, Florida); competes for data-center and industrial sitings and for investor capital.

competitors.name: NextEra Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Florida Power & Light borders Southern's region; NextEra Energy Resources competes with Southern Power in wholesale renewables.

competitors.name: Tennessee Valley Authority
competitors.note: Federal power producer bordering Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi; competes for large industrial and data-center sitings.

competitors.name: Dominion Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Southeast/Virginia regulated utility; the main US data-center hub competing for hyperscaler load.

competitors.name: Entergy Corporation
competitors.note: Neighboring Gulf South utility (Mississippi, Louisiana) competing for industrial and data-center load.

competitors.name: American Electric Power Company, Inc.
competitors.note: Large regulated utility competing for data-center load and transmission projects.

competitors.name: Oglethorpe Power Corporation
competitors.note: Georgia electric membership cooperative generator; Georgia EMCs serve many Georgia customers and can compete for new large loads.

competitors.name: Constellation Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Nuclear and wholesale generation; competes with Southern Power for long-term power contracts.

competitors.name: Vistra Corp.
competitors.note: Competitive generator competing in wholesale power and data-center supply deals.

competitors.name: Atmos Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Regulated gas distributor; peer to Southern Company Gas, including in Tennessee and Virginia.

competitors.name: Spire Inc.
competitors.note: Alabama and Mississippi gas distributor competing with Alabama Power for home heating and cooking energy.

threats: Regulatory and political pushback on bills (Georgia PSC elections, base-rate freeze through 2028) could limit cost recovery or allowed returns.
Data-center demand may fall short of the 75 GW pipeline, leaving costly new gas, solar and battery capacity (10 GW planned at Georgia Power) under-used.
Heavy borrowing for the $81B five-year capital plan: total debt about $75.6B at June 30, 2026 with higher interest costs ($3.24B interest expense in 2025).
Large customers building their own generation or behind-the-meter power, and rooftop solar plus batteries, could erode load.
Storm damage (e.g. Hurricane Helene) and execution risk on large construction projects, as seen with Vogtle 3 and 4 delays and overruns.

ceo.name: Christopher C. Womack
ceo.background: Bachelor's degree from Western Michigan University and master's from The American University; former congressional aide; joined Southern in 1988 and ran HR, generation, external affairs and Georgia Power before becoming CEO in May 2023 (chairman since December 2023)

c1.evidence: Southern is a leader in a mature, century-old industry (regulated utilities); the fast-growing part is data-center load, where it has 10 GW contracted but is one of many utilities serving it.

c2.evidence: Customers mostly 'choose' it because state law grants it exclusive territories in Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi; that advantage is very hard to copy and will likely last decades, but it is not earned by product superiority.

c3.evidence: People in the Southeast know Georgia Power and Alabama Power, but 'Southern Company' itself is not a household name nationally and customers do not choose or recommend it the way they do Google or Netflix.

c4.evidence: Its stated mission ('Providing clean, safe, reliable and affordable energy with excellent service') is repeated consistently and matters for the region's economy, but management is a regulated steward focused on steady earnings rather than a purpose-driven disruptor.

c6.evidence: "Reliable, regulated, Vogtle, rising bills": people see it as a steady, dependable power provider, while bill increases and the over-budget Vogtle project make the impression mixed rather than clearly positive.

c7.evidence: Electricity demand in the Southeast is now growing with AI data centers and manufacturing (large-load sales grew 17% in 2025, commercial sales expected to grow about 20% a year through 2030), but its market is limited to its franchise territories.

c8.evidence: It can grow through data-center supply, PowerSecure microgrids and possibly new nuclear, but it cannot expand its regulated utilities into new states without acquisitions.

m1.evidence: Womack calls 2025 'a transformative year' and has steered an $81B capital plan toward the data-center build-out, but his vision is incremental utility growth rather than a new picture of the future.

m2.evidence: Womack is a career executive who joined Southern in 1988 and became CEO in 2023, a steward rather than a founder.

m4.evidence: He came up through human resources (chief people officer) and emphasises 'Our Values' and customer service, and Georgia Power agreed protections so ordinary customers do not pay for data-center costs.

m5.evidence: Southern's culture is safety- and reliability-focused, well regarded (No. 1 utility in FORTUNE's 2026 Most Admired list), but not built around inventing new products.

m6.evidence: Womack's background is in government affairs, HR and external affairs, not engineering, though he once led Southern Company Generation.

m7.evidence: He is described as a principled leader and serves on community boards (East Lake Foundation, Metro Atlanta Chamber), with stewardship framed around affordable, reliable energy and net-zero by 2050.

m7b.evidence: He gave Oglethorpe University's 2026 commencement address (May 9, 2026), a small Atlanta college rather than a top university like Stanford or Harvard.

m8b.evidence: Womack has a low-key, institutional style with no widely recognized public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2023, Vogtle 4 was completed (April 2024), net income rose from $3,976M (2023) to $4,341M (2025) and operating income from $5,826M to $7,285M, though 2025 diluted EPS slipped to $3.92 from $3.99.

m10.evidence: No notable public record of frugality; as a regulated utility its costs are reviewed by state commissions.

c10.evidence: Its power improves daily life for about 9 million customers and supports the Southeast economy, but it serves one region, not people all over the world.

p2.evidence: Running a reliable grid and building nuclear plants is very hard and vital: Vogtle 3 and 4 were the first new US reactors built from scratch in decades.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 4 of the last 5 years ($20,375M in 2020 to $29,553M in 2025) but fell in 2023 ($29,279M to $25,253M) as fuel and gas costs passed through to customers dropped.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 24.0% in 2020 (4,885/20,375) to 24.7% in 2025 (7,285/29,553), with a dip to 16.0% in 2021; gross margin is swayed by fuel pass-through costs.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 total debt was about $75.6B against cash of $2,984M; equity is positive ($42,342M) but leverage is high, as for most utilities.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $4,885M (2020) to $7,285M (2025), though it fell in 2021 ($3,698M); operating cash flow history was not checked here.

v1.evidence: Electricity is a commodity and customers in its area have no alternative to compare; there is no practical reason to call its product the best in the field.

v2.evidence: It ranked No. 1 among electric and gas utilities in FORTUNE's 2026 World's Most Admired Companies, but it does not appear among the top overall best-places-to-work rankings.

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, about 9 million homes and businesses in the Southeast, plus hospitals, factories and data centers, would lose electricity or gas immediately and notice at once.
